newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refineries face competition challenge.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refineries face competition challenge.

text.p: Refiners in Singapore are gearing up to face the latest challenge in their turbulent history as Asia's refining capacity increases.

A staggering one million barrels per day of new refining capacity would be added to Asia's estimated 15.4 million bpd, even outside the expanding China sector, by the end of the year as new units in South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia start up.
Singapore, the region's swing producer with a refining capacity of 1.23 million bpd, has taken more than its fair share of hits over the years whenever there was a surplus in supplies.

"We can play the role of balancing out disparities in the supply and demand for refined products for markets in the region," said Lim Boon Heng, Singapore's minister without portfolio at a recent industry conference.

But to be able to do this profitably, oil companies have had to be lean and a step ahead of the competition, refiners said. Their latest efforts to stay ahead have led to changes in corporate structures, cost-cutting as prescribed by consultants, and expansion into petrochemicals.
The cost-cutting did not lead to significant job losses. On average, refiners lost about 10 percent of their staff through normal attrition, industry sources said.
The sector employs about 5,000 people.

The only exception was British Petroleum Co Plc, which is laying off 104 people through the shutdown of an old 28,000-bpd refinery last June and the closure of a 200,000 cubic-metre storage terminal on the same site next March.
Oil majors have, however, scaled back less profitable businesses such as bunker operations in the face of emerging bunker ports like Thailand and South Korea.
The companies have shed some time chartered bunker tankers. Mobil Corp has cut back to one barge from two, BP to three from five and Esso Singapore by one to four.
The majors have also given up term storage space for fuel oil, which is used for bunkering.
One refiner said: "The days when we would import fuel oil for bunker sales in Singapore are numbered."
He said it was not economical to continue blending fuel oils to meet Singapore bunker specifications because of high storage and manpower costs.
International oil companies have also restructured their operations to bring decision makers closer to the markets, industry sources said.

Caltex Petroleum Corp, a joint venture between U.S. majors Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp, announced earlier in September plans to move two corporate vice-presidents to Singapore from its head office in the United States.
"We are organising ourselves to be agile and clearly to be in a position to execute strategies within a very prompt time frame," Caltex Chairman David Law-Smith said.
Caltex has a one-third share in a 280,000 bpd refinery that is operated by Singapore Refining Co.
Refiners on the island -- Shell Singapore, Esso, Mobil, BP, Caltex and local-based Singapore Petroleum Co -- are expanding operations upstream, building petrochemical and lubricant plants.

"The trend today is for a greater vertical integration of the petroleum and petrochemical operations as this increases overall plant efficiency and takes advantage of the synergy that exists between the two business sectors," Lim said.
Such investments have amounted to several billion dollars.
Mobil started up a world-scale paraxylene plant in 1994 and is spending US$200 million to double this capacity in 1998 to 700,000 tonnes a year.
It is also investing US$200 million to build a lube-based oil plant to start in late 1997, and is studying the feasibility of a US$1 billion, 800,000-tonne ethylene plant.
Shell, with a one-third stake in the Petrochemical Corp of Singapore (PCS), the island's sole ethylene producer, is involved in a US$1.8 billion expansion to double PCS's capacity.
In early 1997, Shell will start up a styrene monomer/propylene oxide plant costing some US$500 million.

Refiners say that for now, profits are under pressure, but prospects for the coming years are much better because the latest Asian refinery expansions are expected to be the last for two to four years.

Also, plans to set up preferential tariffs for trade within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) would give Singapore refiners an edge over products imported from outside ASEAN, they said.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesian, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and new member Vietnam.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3093)
